p.seg: Although an ordinary person has an inborn nature,
their mind lacks a settled will.
TZL It relies on external things
and only then is it stirred to action;
TZL it relies on what is pleasing
and only then does it act;
TZL it relies on habit
and only then does it become settled.
The energies of joy, anger, sorrow, and grief
are the inborn nature.
When they are manifested externally,
it is because external things have elicited them.
The inborn nature comes forth from the endowment,
and the endowment descends from Heaven.
The Way (Dào) begins in the feelings,
and the feelings arise from the inborn nature.
The beginning is close to the feelings;
the culmination is close to righteousness.
One who understands the feelings is able to express them;
one who understands rightness (yì) is able to internalize it.
Liking and disliking,
are innate nature (xìng).
That which is liked and that which is disliked,
are things.
To deem good,
and not deeming good,
are innate nature (xìng)],
that which is deemed good
and that which is deemed not good,
are circumstances.
In all cases, innate nature (xìng) is the master,
and things are what it selects.
SM As for the sound that is in metal and stone,
if they are not struck,
they do not sound].
Although there is an innate nature (xìng),
if the heart-mind (xīn) does not engage with it,
it is not expressed.
In all cases, the heart-mind (xīn) has intention.
DYZ To be without interaction with others
is not permissible;
[a person cannot] act alone,
just as a mouth cannot speak alone.
An ox is born and grows long;
a wild goose is born and stretches out;
. their nature [causes it to be so].
[A person], however, learns.
is because something causes them to do so.
Of all things, there are none that are not different.
LL A pillar [tree] is established for its hardness;
it is selected for its hardness.
A cord is used for binding due to its flexibility;
it is selected for its flexibility.
Within the four seas, their nature (xìng) is one and the same.
Their use of mind is different in each case;
teaching is what makes it so.
Regarding nature (xìng), in all cases:
something may move it,
or oppose it,
or interact with it,
or hone it,
or bring it out,
or nourish it,
or cause it to grow.
That which moves nature,
is external things.
That which opposes nature,
is pleasure.
That which interacts with nature,
is precedent.
That which hones nature,
is righteousness (yì).
That which brings nature out,
is the circumstances (shì).
That which nourishes nature,
is custom;
That which allows human nature to develop
is the Way.
All that is perceived is called 'things';
that which is pleasing to oneself is called 'pleasure';
the inherent tendency of things is called 'the situation';
that which is an intentional act is called 'cause'.
Rightness
is the root-cluster of all goodness.
Custom
is the means by which one practices their nature.
The Way
is the way of all things.
In all ways,
the art of the mind is primary.
There are four arts of the Way,
and only the Way of Man
can be articulated as a path.
As for the other three arts,
they are merely to be followed.
The *Odes*, the *Documents*, the *Rites*, and the *Music*—
in their origins, they all arose from man.
The *Odes*
are intentional,
SHR1168.6 an act of [哦: n ] making.
The *Documents*
are intentional,
an act of stating.
Rites and Music,
are created for a purpose;
this is to put them into practice.
The Sages group them by category
and discuss them collectively,
observe their sequence
and explain them by tracing them back to their origins,
embody their meaning
and give them sequence and form,
put their essential feelings in order
and regulate their expression,
and only then do they in turn use them to teach.
Teaching,
is that by which virtue is engendered within.
The Rites,
arise from essential feelings;
some are prompted by change.
They correspond to the matter at hand
and are based on the local customs,
and are thus formulated.
Their sequence of precedence
is the way of propriety.
Some have a set sequence;
to create regulations for them
is to give them cultural form.
Perfecting one's bearing and appearance,
is the means by which to give them cultural form;
it is a matter of regulation.
The gentleman (jūnzǐ) holds his inner nature to be beautiful,
values his sense of rightness,
perfects his adherence to regulations,
is fond of his proper bearing,
takes joy in his Way,
and is pleased with his teachings.
For this reason, he is respected.
Bowing
is the means by which one shows submission.
Its deferential measure
is cultural refinement.
Gifts of silk
are the means by which one shows sincerity and provides a token;
the words accompanying them, when presented,
should be appropriate to the Way of righteousness.
Laughter
is the shallow moistening of ritual.
Music
is the deep moistening of ritual.
As for all sounds,
only when their issuance from one's inner nature is authentic
will their entering and stirring a person's heart-mind be profound.
Upon hearing the sound of laughter,
one feels refreshed and bright,
and so is joyful.
Upon hearing songs and ballads,
one feels a contented expansiveness.
and are stirred.
When listening to the sounds of the `qín` and `sè` zithers,
they are moved,
and they sigh.
When observing the *Lài* and the *Wǔ*,
they become solemn,
and are stirred to action.
When observing the *Sháo* and the *Xià*,
LL then they become modest and respectful,
QXG and are composed.
They chant and reflect,
and their hearts are moved;
they sigh deeply.
LZSHR1179.9 Their adherence to proper measure
is long-practiced;
their return to goodness
and beginning anew
is cautious.
Their conduct in all matters
is orderly;
DYZSHR1180.12 they thereby take charge of their virtue.
As for the music of Zhèng and Wèi,
people follow sounds that are improper
and are led astray by them.
LZ In all cases, ancient music engages the heart;
LZ the music of Yì engages the fingers.
Both are things that instruct a person.
The music of the *Lài* and the *Wǔ* is about taking,
the music of *Sháo* and *Xià* is about inner feeling.
In all cases, the ultimate music is necessarily sorrowful.
Weeping is also sorrowful.
Both reach the extremity of feeling.
Sorrow and joy—
their natures are similar,
and for this reason the states of mind they produce are not far apart.
When weeping moves the heart-mind,
it gradually subsides.
LL Its intensity is lingering and reluctant,
and it ends in mournfulness.
When music moves the heart-mind,
DYZ it is profound and filled with pent-up feeling.
LL Its intensity
DYZ then becomes mournful,
leading to sadness,
and becomes distant,
leading to contemplation.
In all cases, anxious contemplation
is followed by sorrow.
In all cases, joyful contemplation
is followed by happiness.
In all cases, the exertion of the heart-mind in contemplation
is most intense.
A sigh
is the expression of contemplation.
When its sound changes,
then [the heart-mind follows it],
when its heart-mind changes,
then its sound is also thus.
LZLL: chanting is from sorrow;
LZ: clamor is from joy;
DYZLZ: the sorrowful sound is from the voice;
LLLZ: a deep sigh is from the heart-mind.
Joy leads to contentment;
contentment leads to being roused;
being roused leads to singing;
singing leads to swaying;
swaying leads to dancing.
Dancing
is the culmination of joy.
Resentment leads to worry;
worry leads to grief;
grief leads to sighing;
sighing leads to beating the breast;
beating the breast leads to stamping the feet.
Stamping the feet
is the culmination of resentment.
For any learner,
grasping the inner state is difficult.
By following the outward expression,
one comes close to grasping it,
but this is not as quick as using music.
Although one may be able to perform the action,
if one cannot grasp its inner state,
it is not valued.
If in seeking their state of mind
there is pretense,
you will fail to grasp it.
That a person cannot maintain pretense indefinitely
is knowable.
In no more than ten instances,
their true mind will surely be revealed;
by observing what is thus revealed,
how can their genuine state be missed?
`Shù` (reciprocity)
is the method for `yì` (righteousness).
`Yì` (righteousness)
is the method for `jìng` (reverence).
`Jìng` (reverence)
is the proper articulation of things.
`Dǔ` (sincerity)
is the method for `rén` (benevolence).
`Rén` (benevolence)
is the method of `xìng` (human nature).
It is human nature that gives rise to it.
`Zhōng` (conscientiousness)
is the method for `xìn` (trustworthiness).
`Xìn` (trustworthiness)
is the method for `qíng` (genuine feelings).
`Qíng` (genuine feelings) come from `xìng` (human nature).
There are seven kinds of love;
only the love that is rooted in one's nature (`xìng ài`)
is close to `rén` (benevolence).
There are five types of wisdom;
only the way of righteousness (yìdào)
is close to loyalty (zhōng).
There are three types of hatred;
only hating what is not benevolent
is close to righteousness (yì).
Of the things called the Way, there are four;
only the Human Way (réndào)
is the one that can be followed.
For those whose use of the mind is agitated,
thinking is the most intense aspect.
For those whose use of wisdom is hasty,
trouble is the most severe result.
For those whose use of emotion is extreme,
sorrow and joy are the most intense.
LL For those whose use of the body is agile,
pleasure is the most intense sensation.
For those whose use of strength is exhaustive,
personal gain is the most extreme outcome.
The eye's love of beautiful forms,
the ear's delight in pleasant sounds—
these are a kind of pent-up energy;
people do not find it difficult to die for them.
If a person's conduct is all meticulous and showy,
but they do not possess a straightforward heart,
then it is mere ornamentation.
If a person's conduct is one of great simplicity,

LLGDE but they do not possess a will that is constant (恒 héng, glossed as 終 zhōng) and harmonious (怡 yí, given as a correction for 始 shǐ, which in turn corrects 殆 dài)...* *** *Note: This final sentence is a fragment in the source text.*
then they are unfocused.
As for those who are clever with words and sharp in speech,
if they do not possess a humble and yielding mind,
then they are merely glib.
As for those who are so agreeable that one can be with them in peace and harmony,
if they do not possess a spirit of vigorous striving,
[LL] then they are muddled (variant: neglectful).
There are those whose character is straightforward and incisive;
[LL] if they are not cultivated (variant: shepherded),
they are unacceptable.
SHR1216.12 There are those whose character is profound (variant `原` yuán);
if they are unsupported,
they are insufficient.
In general, human artifice is detestable.
Artifice leads to pettiness;
pettiness leads to suspicious calculation;
and suspicious calculation leads to no one forming bonds with them.
Caution
is the method of benevolence (rén).
However, its excess is not vile.
Speed
is the method of strategy;
an excess in it, however, results in disaster.
If a person is not cautious,
they will then be excessively trusting.
In general, human nature
is something to be delighted in.
If one acts solely according to that nature,...
even if one is at fault,
one is not disliked.
If one does not act in accordance with their disposition,
it will be difficult.
Even if one is not of high rank,
if they truly have sincerity,
even if they have not yet acted,
they will certainly be trusted.
To be trusted before speaking
is to be one who has a fine disposition.
For the people to be constant before being taught
is the mark of one whose nature is good.
For the people to be encouraged before being rewarded
is the mark of one who embodies blessings.
For the people to be in awe before punishments are used
is the mark of one who has an inner majesty.
To be of low status, yet have the people value you,
is to be one who has virtue.
To be poor, yet have the people gather to you,
is to be one who has the Way.
To be happy when alone
is to be one who has internalized ritual propriety.
To be disliked
yet unable to be criticized
is to be one who is an expert in righteousness.
To be criticized
yet unable to be disliked
is to be one who is devoted to benevolence.
One whose actions are not excessive
is one who knows the Way.
One who, upon hearing the Way, reflects upon their superiors
is one who associates with those above.
One who, upon hearing the Way, reflects upon their inferiors
is one who associates with those below.
One who, upon hearing the Way, reflects upon themself
is one who cultivates the self.
Associating with superiors is close to serving a ruler.
Associating with those below and winning over the masses is close to engaging in governance.
Cultivating the self is close to achieving ultimate benevolence.
To associate with those of the same principles
is to do so based on the Way.
To associate with those of different principles
is to do so based on prior connections.
To associate with those with whom one is mutually pleased
is to do so based on virtue.
To associate with those with whom one is not mutually pleased
is to do so based on counsel.
In the governance of the household,
SHR1197.13LL one desires that its faults be concealed.
In governance outside the household,
one desires that it be systematic.
When praising others,
do not be stingy.
Your own actions must be consistent with it,
and when the topic
is raised, mention them explicitly.
and do not be insincere.
In all interactions, do not be too intense;
you must ensure they have a future.
LLGDE Whenever on the road, do not be anxious,
and do not speak to yourself.
When dwelling alone,
then practice what your father and elder brothers enjoy.
If it causes no great harm,
it is acceptable to bend a little to go along with it.
Once it is done, do not speak of it again.
In matters of sorrow and hardship, one should seek to take them on;
in joyful matters, one should seek to be last.
SHR1179.14LL The body should be still and not agitated.
SHR1198.16 Deliberations should be deep and not rash.
Actions should be brave and must see things through to the end.
LL One's bearing should be dignified and not arrogant.
The [mind] should be gentle, orderly, and tranquil.
Joy should be expressed with wisdom and have no negative consequences.
LL Pleasure should be savored and have purpose.
Sorrow should be restrained and not lead to a clouded mind.
GDELL Anger should be fully acknowledged and not concealed.
When advancing, one should be modest and not devious.
XLLDYZ When retreating, one should be cautious and not hasty.
LL In all these, one should be adroit and not artificial.
